item.title: Casa to get repairs in Indonesia
item.description: PNG Defence Force CASA CN-235 aircraft, P2-502 ready to depart for Indonesia (NBC News) Papua New Guinea is taking steps to restore its military air transport capability after years of relying on external support to move personnel and equipment.
item.content:encoded:
PNG Defence Force CASA CN-235 aircraft, P2-502 ready to depart for Indonesia (NBC News)

Papua New Guinea is taking steps to restore its military air transport capability after years of relying on external support to move personnel and equipment.

The PNG Defence Force CASA CN-235 aircraft, P2-502, has departed for Indonesia for major servicing and a complete overhaul under the CASA Recovery Programme.

Prime Minister James Marape says restoring the aircraft will strengthen national security, border protection and disaster response.

PNG Defence Force Commander Rear Admiral Philip Polewara says restoring the aircraft will strengthen the military's ability to safeguard the country and assist communities during disasters.

The aircraft is expected to return to PNG in time to support next year's General Elections.

item.title: Fuel price rise adds pressure on Lae businesses and PMV operators
item.description: Rising fuel prices are putting additional pressure on businesses and public motor vehicle (PMV) operators in Lae, with higher operating costs also affecting transport fares and the prices of goods and services. Businesses that depend on diesel generators to keep their operations running are among those feeling the impact, particularly as unreliable electricity supply forces some to rely on generat
item.content:encoded:
Rising fuel prices are putting additional pressure on businesses and public motor vehicle (PMV) operators in Lae, with higher operating costs also affecting transport fares and the prices of goods and services.

Businesses that depend on diesel generators to keep their operations running are among those feeling the impact, particularly as unreliable electricity supply forces some to rely on generators for extended periods.

Lae Chamber of Commerce and Industry President John Byrne says the combination of rising fuel costs and power supply problems is making it more expensive for businesses to operate.

Byrne says some businesses run diesel generators around the clock, while others maintain backup generators to avoid disruptions when electricity supply is unreliable.

A PMV driver in Lae says the increase is also affecting daily transport operations.

The driver says K50 previously bought about 10 litres of fuel, but the same amount now buys only six litres, making it harder to keep the vehicle operating and earn an income.

The driver says the reduced amount of fuel is affecting daily work, as more money is needed to keep the vehicle on the road. Byrne says PMV operators often respond to rising fuel prices by increasing fares, adding to the cost of travelling for passengers.

He says higher transport and operating costs eventually affect businesses and consumers, as businesses adjust their prices to meet increased expenses.

Byrne also says the fuel price increases are driven by external factors and are not something the Government directly controls. However, he believes businesses will have to adjust to the higher costs, saying he would be surprised if companies were already considering closing their operations because of the increases.

The rising fuel costs come at a time when businesses in Lae are also dealing with unreliable power supply, increasing pressure on their operating budgets.

item.title: WCS strengthens community conservation efforts
item.description: Participants attended the Inter-CBO workshop at Yasina. (Supplied) The Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) has brought together nine community-based conservation organisations for the first time at Yasina, Ungai-Bena District, Eastern Highlands, to strengthen collaboration and protect biodiversity across the Bismarck Forest Corridor.
item.content:encoded:
Participants attended the Inter-CBO workshop at Yasina. (Supplied)

The Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) has brought together nine community-based conservation organisations for the first time at Yasina, Ungai-Bena District, Eastern Highlands, to strengthen collaboration and protect biodiversity across the Bismarck Forest Corridor.

WCS Senior Community Relations Manager, Bennie Atigini says the workshop brings the inter Community Based Organisations (CBOs) representatives together to build resilience in their respective conservation areas.

“The workshop aims to strengthen networks, promote the exchange conservation knowledge and support sustainable management of biodiversity and natural resources across the Bismarck forest corridor.

“We have brought CBO leaders together to share their experiences over the past 12 months, discuss their challenges and identify ways we can collaborate as an organisation to implement conservation programmes and support livelihood activities on the ground,” Bennie said.

He says the Wild-Life Conservation society is trying to create an avenue to build governance structures for CBO’s groups and understand the challenges and work together to address them in their respective CBO’s and their communities.

Mt Dorohere Conservation Area representative Stephanie Alois says the workshop has strengthened her understanding of governance and livelihood programmes to better support communities and conservation efforts.

“Conservation is a big responsibility, and everyone must play their part in protecting our forests and water sources.”

Speaking as a young conservation advocate, Stephanie is urging youths to take an active role in community development and conservation to protect their natural resources for future generations.

“My message to young people is to take part in community activities such as agriculture and conservation. We must take responsibility because we are the ones who will lead our communities in the future,” she said.

The workshop brought together six established conservation areas and three emerging sites across Madang, Eastern Highlands, Chimbu and Jiwaka provinces, all within the Bismarck Forest Corridor.

item.title: New Censorship policy targets online content
item.description: Participants and stakeholders at the two-day workshop on censorship policy and online content regulation, bringing together representatives from government agencies, NICTA, the media, churches and other organisations to discuss the implementation and implications of censorship policy in Papua New Guinea (NBC News) Papua New Guinea's proposed National Censorship Policy III (2027–2031) will address
item.content:encoded:
Participants and stakeholders at the two-day workshop on censorship policy and online content regulation, bringing together representatives from government agencies, NICTA, the media, churches and other organisations to discuss the implementation and implications of censorship policy in Papua New Guinea (NBC News)

Papua New Guinea's proposed National Censorship Policy III (2027–2031) will address the growing challenges of regulating harmful online content as the use of digital platforms continues to increase.

The policy was discussed during a two-day Momase and Highlands Regional Consultative Workshop held at Lae International Hotel on November 11 and 12.

Chief Censor Jim Abani said the new policy would move beyond traditional censorship and respond to changes in how people access, produce and distribute information through the internet.

Abani said the Censorship Office was working towards a framework that would address online content, including material that could expose children and young people to harmful information.

He revealed that more than 33,000 websites containing harmful content had been submitted to the National Information and Communications Technology Authority (NICTA), while more than 200,000 websites had been listed as blocked.

The role of NICTA in supporting the proposed censorship framework was also discussed during the workshop.

NICTA's presentation highlighted the regulatory processes involved in restricting access to harmful websites and the importance of addressing online content through established legal and regulatory mechanisms.

The discussions also considered the challenges of internet access and the growing availability of online services, which have increased the need for an updated approach to censorship.

The proposed policy recognises that censorship can no longer focus only on traditional materials such as films, publications and other physical content, but must also consider material distributed through digital platforms.

The consultation brought together stakeholders from the Momase and Highlands regions to provide input into the proposed policy before it guides the country's censorship framework for 2027 to 2031.

The policy is expected to provide direction on how Papua New Guinea responds to harmful content while addressing the challenges created by changes in technology and online communication.

item.title: Australia continues to support PNG’s Law and Justice sector
item.description: Acting Counsellor for Law and Justice Sector with the Australian High Commission, Nicholas Yates chatting with Madang Governor, Ramsey Pariwa after the official opening of the Reflection Workshop on Wednesday (NBC News) Australia has re-affirmed its commitment to PNG's Law and Justice Sector.
item.content:encoded:
Acting Counsellor for Law and Justice Sector with the Australian High Commission, Nicholas Yates chatting with Madang Governor, Ramsey Pariwa after the official opening of the Reflection Workshop on Wednesday (NBC News)

Australia has re-affirmed its commitment to PNG's Law and Justice Sector.

The Acting Counsellor for Law and Justice Sector with the Australian High Commission, Nicholas Yates said this during the second day of a reflection workshop for the Law and Justice sector in Madang Province.

Addressing participants of the workshop, he said Australia is a good friend to Papua New Guinea, and both countries have worked together to strengthen safety, justice, governance and service delivery across the country.

"Through the Australia- PNG Law and Justice Partnership (APLJ), Australia supports PNG's vision for a fair, effective and accessible justice system that serves all citizens, including those in rural and remote communities.

"Australia's support extends across the law and justice sector, working alongside national, provincial and local institutions to strengthen coordination, leadership, and service delivery. This includes support to the different levels of the court system, the police, correctional services, community justice mechanisms, and the institutions responsible for addressing family and sexual violence, promoting community safety and improving access to justice," said Mr Yates.

He went on to also explain that Australia's role is not to direct or lead these efforts.

Rather, its role is to work alongside PNG counterpart in helping to strengthen local capacity, support reforms that are driven by PNG priorities, and foster partnerships that deliver practical outcomes for communities.

Mr Yates further told the participants, mainly village court officials, district administrators, llg managers, police and CS officers that they are the first point of contact for members of their communities who face conflicts, disputes and challenges.

"Your continuous engagement with your communities helps to strengthen law and order and ensure that everyone feels safe and protected.

"We recognise that effective law and justice services depend not only on strong national insitutions, but also on strong provincial leadership and community- led engagements.

"The workshop this week is an important opportunity for you to share your experiences with each other, to boost collaboration with your peers and to strengthen to coordination between all law and justice stakeholders in the province.

"I know that many of you work in remote locations, so please take the time whilst you are together to build strong relationships with each other. These foundations will support you all to better serve your communities," he said.

Mr Yates also highlighted that such gatherings are so important as they provide an opportunity to bring together those responsible for delivering services on the ground, to discuss common challenges, share practical solutions, and identify opportunities to work more effectively as one sector.

He said Australia is proud to support this work under the Australia- PNG Law and Justice Partnership program.

Also, in attendance at the meeting this week is the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) Deputy Commissioner, Thomas Eluh, who did a presentation on the work ICAC is doing in the country, Madang's new PPC, Chief Superintendent Vakaruru Uraia, and the Senior Provincial Magistrate, Fridolin Kambibel, who is also the Chairman of the Provincial Land Dispute Committee, and Deputy Provincial Administrator, Michael Pamaraka.

The meeting was officially opened by Madang Governor, Ramsey Pariwa on Wednesday.

Pariwa re- assured the law and justice sector in Madang of his government's continuous support.

"My duty, the provincial government's duty, DDA's duty, and our political leaders' duty at the sub- national level of government is to support you. The actual work of implementing and enforcing the law, implementing the policies of government is with the law and justice sector.

"And I am grateful all of you are here because I've already started the work of empowering and supporting our law and justice sector in the province.

"I'm looking forward to see if we can build a new courthouse for both the national and district court. I'd like to see that we build a new police station at Jomba too, and improve the facilities at Beon CS, but we need partners," Governor Pariwa said.

item.title: Banak high school celebrates historic first Grade 10 graduation
item.description: The 59-pioneer grade 10 students of Banak high school in Boikin LLG, Wewak district (Supplied) Banak Junior High School in Boikin Local-Level Government (LLG), Wewak district, marked a milestone on tuesday with its first Grade 10 graduation where fifty-nine students graduated as the school's pioneer class.
item.content:encoded:
The 59-pioneer grade 10 students of Banak high school in Boikin LLG, Wewak district (Supplied)

Banak Junior High School in Boikin Local-Level Government (LLG), Wewak district, marked a milestone on tuesday with its first Grade 10 graduation where fifty-nine students graduated as the school's pioneer class.

The occassion, held under the theme, "Celebrating Achievements, Inspiring the future", brought together locals from neighboring villages in both Boikin and Dagua LLG to celebrate the establishment and growth of Boikin LLG's newest high school. Otto Sauiembi, a long-serving Board Chairman of the school, applauded the students for setting the legacy of the school.

"Thank you for making us proud", he said.

Joining him to congratulate the pioneer class, keynote speaker and Wewak District's Primary School Inspector Vincent Illowen also shared similar remarks. "Beat the garamut! Banak has a high school that is here to stay", Illowen said.

During his keynote speech, he challenged the teachers to produce exceptional students as Banak High School has the potential of creating quality education.

Illowen was acknowledged by Sauiembi and the pioneer principal of the school, Richard Kaus, for getting this new school registered.

Banak Junior High School's success was also alluded to the pioneer head teacher, Richard Kaus.

A representative from the Education Division of East Sepik Raphael Borungai, applauded Kaus for taking on the challenge in bringing up the new school.

He said Kaus also set a similar record at the current Moem Junior High School in Wewak.

This milestone occasion for the people of Boikin and Dagua LLG, shows the strong support and collaboration between staff, students and the locals.

item.title: Catholic Church calls for online child protection
item.description: Fr John Joseph of the Catholic Diocese of Lae (Supplied) The Catholic Church is calling for stronger protection of children and young people from harmful online content, saying parents, churches and schools must play a greater role in guiding them.
item.content:encoded:
Fr John Joseph of the Catholic Diocese of Lae (Supplied)

The Catholic Church is calling for stronger protection of children and young people from harmful online content, saying parents, churches and schools must play a greater role in guiding them.

Fr John Joseph of the Catholic Diocese of Lae raised the concern during the National Censorship Policy Workshop in Lae, where discussions focused on protecting children and young people in the digital space.

Fr Joseph says children as young as seven and eight years old are already exposed to inappropriate material online.

He says the church places strong emphasis on the formation of children and young people to help them develop positive values and make responsible choices.

The church's approach focuses on religious education and guiding young people through Christian teachings.

Fr Joseph says the church believes in strengthening children's understanding of Gospel values as they grow up in a changing digital environment.

He says protecting children from harmful online content requires a shared effort involving parents, churches, schools, communities and government agencies.

The call comes as Papua New Guinea continues discussions on strengthening censorship measures and addressing the risks children face when accessing online platforms.

item.title: Preparation begins for 36th Lutheran Synod in 2028
item.description: (L-R) Rev Lukas Kedabing-Assistant Bishop, Rev Bon Nelson-Madang District President, Ramsey Pariwa-Madang Governor & Synod Patron, Daniel Aloi-Synod Planning committee Chairman, Rev. Francis Ambuk-represents History and Pr Reina Kubong-represents future church (NBC News) A groundbreaking was held recently in Madang, marking the commencement of preparatory work by the Lutheran Church in the provinc
item.content:encoded:
(L-R) Rev Lukas Kedabing-Assistant Bishop, Rev Bon Nelson-Madang District President, Ramsey Pariwa-Madang Governor & Synod Patron, Daniel Aloi-Synod Planning committee Chairman, Rev. Francis Ambuk-represents History and Pr Reina Kubong-represents future church (NBC News)

A groundbreaking was held recently in Madang, marking the commencement of preparatory work by the Lutheran Church in the province towards hosting the Church's 36th National Synod in January 2028.

The ceremony was held at Nagada Plantation, an old plantation owned by the Lutheran Church, towards the north coast.

Nagada will be the central location or site for the 2028 Synod.

Madang Governor Ramsey Pariwa and Provincial Administrator, Daniel Aloi, were joined by senior clergymen from the church; Rev. Lucas Kedabing, Assistant Bishop of ELC- PNG, Rev. Bon Nelson - District President of Madang, Pastor Francis Ambuk, representing older pastors in Madang and Pastor Reiner Kubong, representing younger pastors, in the ceremony.

The event was witnessed by the General Secretary of ELC- PNG, Bernard Kaisum, Lutheran faithfuls, and the general public.

Mr Kaisum emphasised the importance of the upcoming synod, stating it will be the first for the next 50 years; both in the Church's calendar and the country's journey after independence.

The groundbreaking was followed by the unveiling of a huge billboard at the Nagada Junction, which declares that the next 50 years for ELC- PNG begins at Nagada, which will be the site of the 2028 Synod.

He also expressed gratitude to the local working committee, headed by Chairman and Madang's Provincial Administrator, Daniel Aloi; for starting the ground work early.

"People of Madang, you must be prepared for the Synod. As host, we must prepare the groundwork. It's gonna be a lot of hard work, but we must work with absolute faith in God that we can do it.

"We, from the headquarters; are happy to see those of you who have come to witness this special occasion. You represent the thousands of Lutheran faithfuls in this province who can not make it here to witness this event.

"The Synod will test our transport systems, and our ability to host such big event so we must be well prepared," Mr Kaisum said.

Chairman of the local organising committee and Madang's Provincial Administrator, Daniel Aloi, said it's a long road ahead for the committee.

"We have come this far with no political or business support. This is only one part of the Synod, and I can't think of any other way to do this but to continue to pray. What we are doing is like what John the Baptist did; preparing the groundwork for the Synod.

"We report to the Madang District Council, and we all must have a responsibility in this," he said.

Mr Aloi added that the committee is going ahead with the preparation despite critics from certain people that Madang is not ready to host the Synod.

Governor Ramsey Pariwa, meanwhile, was not happy that it has taken a long time for the groundwork to begin.

"It's been nine months since the last Synod ended in Siassi, Morobe Province and we brought the Synod shield to Madang. I am not happy that it took us this long to make decisions and start working. We have delayed work by nine months, and we cannot afford to waste any more time. It's time to work," Governor Pariwa stated.

He added that God has a plan for Madang, and the people must be ready to receive what He has to give.

Pariwa said, "Madang has not hosted a Synod in many years. We have been roaming in the wilderness, indulging ourselves in too many ungodly things like killing and cutting; and law, and order has deteriorated.

"We have played too much Church politics, and this must stop now. God wants to visit us, and we can't stop Him. Church politics has destroyed the church. Put your differences aside, and start working together. We are not here to please anybody. This is God's business."

Governor Pariwa is the Patron of the 36th Lutheran Synod.
